name: Question 2
worked_solution:
The stationary points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T},$ where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+y-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2y+x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x+y-3 & 2y+x+3\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the stationary points, we need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$
Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+y-3=0 \\ 2y+x+3=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $y$ in the first equation, we get

$$
2x+y-3=0\,⟹\,y=3-2x.
$$

Then, substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2(3-2x)+x+3 & =0 \\ 6-4x+x+3 & =0 \\ 9-3x & =0 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting this value into $y=3-2x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y=3-2(3)=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our system has one solution, $(3,-3).$ 

In conclusion, $f$ has one stationary point, $(3,-3).$

In this case, the domain of f is R2, and the first partial derivatives of f are ∂f∂x=2x+y−3∂f∂y=2y+x+3.

Solving for y in the first equation, we get 2x+y−3=0⟹y=3−2x.

Back-substituting this value into y=3−2x, we get y=3−2(3)=−3.
